Date: 2026-02-26
Time: 15:00 PT

Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samantha Lee (CTO, Halcyon), Raj Patel (Lead Platform Eng), Marta Gomez (Security Architect), Evan Brooks (DevOps)

Notes: discovery focused on Private/VPC deployment networking, peering, private endpoints and region constraints; asked for pricing/TCO and network templates
summary: Customer is evaluating Private (VPC) deployment for PHI workloads. Main concerns: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, cross-region limitations, CIDR constraints, egress paths, KMS integration, and SOC2/audit log requirements. Redwood AE/SE recommended topology options and will follow up with pricing, network diagrams and example infra snippets. Customer timeline: Q2 pilot, production by Q3 contingent on compliance and region support.
topics: Network topology options: VPC peering vs PrivateLink/Private Endpoints
Cross-region constraints (AWS vs GCP vs Azure)
KMS/HSM and key management for model data
Audit logs, SSO and SOC2 controls
Dedicated vs Private TCO and latency tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 45 minutes. Quick intros from our side: I'm Alex, AE at Redwood.
[00:06] Priya Nair: Hi all, Priya here, I'm the solutions engineer, I'll dig into the network stuff.
[00:10] Samantha Lee: Sam here, CTO at Halcyon. We're evaluating private deployments for some PHI pipelines.
[00:14] Raj Patel: Raj, I'll be owning the infra side.
[00:16] Marta Gomez: Marta, security. Thanks for doing this.
[00:18] Alex Chen: Great. The goal for today is to understand your constraints - networking, regions, compliance - and outline next steps. Priya, do you want to kick into the topology options?
[00:28] Priya Nair: Sure. So there are two common approaches we see: one is VPC peering/transit gateway where we peer your VPC with Redwood's private VPC, and the other is private endpoints - e.g., AWS PrivateLink or Azure Private Endpoint - where traffic goes over private endpoints into Redwood services. Each has tradeoffs.
[00:45] Raj Patel: Quick Q: With peering are we opening up routing between our entire VPCs? We have pretty tight CIDR constraints, small ranges.
[00:52] Priya Nair: Good question. Peering requires route entries and non-overlapping CIDRs. If your CIDR overlaps or you want more isolation, PrivateLink is safer because it exposes specific interfaces. Peering + transit gateway can work but you need planned CIDR sizes and route propagation.
[01:10] Marta Gomez: Our security team hates broad peering; we can't allow arbitrary routing to Redwood. We'd prefer endpoint-level access, or at minimum strict subnet and security group controls. Also, we have to use our KMS for any customer-managed keys.
[01:22] Alex Chen: Redwood supports customer-managed keys via KMS integration for Private. We can integrate with your AWS KMS or bring-your-own HSM in some private deployments. We'll capture specifics after this call.
[01:30] Samantha Lee: Region-wise, we need a deployment in us-east-1 for latency to our main services, but we also have a European data residency requirement for some datasets. How does Redwood handle multi-region?
[01:39] Priya Nair: Our Private option supports deployments in multiple regions, but note that not all hardware profiles are available in every region. For example, certain GPU-backed clusters we recommend for low-latency transformer inference may be in us-east-1 and us-west-2; Europe availability depends on capacity. We can do a primary in us-east-1 and a separate EU private deployment for data residency, or route only EU traffic to the EU instance.
[02:05] Raj Patel: If we spin up two private deployments, is there cross-region peering between Redwood-managed VPCs or do we handle egress?
[02:12] Priya Nair: Typically separate deployments mean separate VPCs. We can peer them internally, but cross-region peering has limitations. On AWS, VPC peering supports cross-region but latency and egress costs vary. For EU-residency data, best practice is keep data in-region and avoid cross-region egress.
[02:30] Evan Brooks: What about PrivateLink? Is that available cross-region, or would we need endpoints in each region?
[02:36] Priya Nair: PrivateLink endpoints are regional. You'd need a private endpoint in each region to hit that regional Redwood control plane.
[02:42] Marta Gomez: On audit logs and compliance, we need an immutable stream of access logs for model requests, ideally pushed to our S3 with lifecycle rules. Does Redwood provide that?
[02:51] Alex Chen: Yes, in Private we can configure audit logs and integrate with your logging pipeline. We support pushing logs to customer-owned S3 buckets, and we have structured event logs that map requests to tokens, timestamps, and model versions. We'll share the event schema.
[03:06] Samantha Lee: Ok. Also SSO - we use SAML via Okta and need SCIM provisioning.
[03:11] Priya Nair: We support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning in the Private control plane. There's an admin role mapping and RBAC.
[03:18] Raj Patel: Network NAT and egress - where does outbound traffic go? We need to ensure egress goes through our firewall and that egress IPs are whitelisted in some downstream APIs.
[03:27] Priya Nair: For Private, you can route egress through your NAT/gateway. If you're peering, your route table can send outbound traffic to your transit. If using PrivateLink, egress from the endpoint still originates from Redwood's subnet unless you configure hairpin or custom NAT via your VPC. We'll send a diagram showing standard egress flows.
[03:48] Marta Gomez: Any specifics about DNS resolution? We run split-horizon DNS internally.
[03:53] Priya Nair: We recommend using your internal DNS to resolve private endpoints. For PrivateLink you create an interface endpoint and configure private DNS to point to that ENI. With peering, you'd need conditional forwarding for Redwood's hostnames or private hosted zones shared via Route53. There are a few patterns, we'll include examples.
[04:17] Samantha Lee: Are there IP range recommendations? We only have two /16s left in our org - limited space.
[04:23] Alex Chen: Peering requires non-overlapping ranges; if space is tight, PrivateLink is usually better because it doesn't require allocating new large CIDRs on our side. Also we offer NAT mapping options.
[04:34] Raj Patel: From a latency perspective, how does Private compare to Dedicated?
[04:39] Priya Nair: Dedicated is reserved capacity in our hosted environment - it's great for predictable throughput and lower multi-tenant variance. Private (VPC) gives you network locality benefits and data isolation, but performance depends on the chosen instance types and network hop counts. If you deploy Private in the same region and minimize hops - e.g., within a VPC peered or via PrivateLink - latencies are very comparable. We'll give benchmark examples.
[05:04] Samantha Lee: For PHI we need encryption in transit and at rest. Do you support TLS mutual auth between our services and Redwood endpoints?
[05:11] Priya Nair: Yes, TLS is mandatory. We can do mTLS on Private if you require client certs for additional assurance. We'll need to exchange certs/CA details and map them to accounts.
[05:22] Marta Gomez: KMS - can we bring our keys? We need CMEK for model artifact encryption.
[05:27] Alex Chen: Yes, customer-managed keys are supported. For some deployments we can integrate with your AWS KMS key policy or use HSM-backed keys. There are additional compliance steps for HSMs but it's doable.
[05:38] Raj Patel: A practical ask: can you share a sample Terraform template showing how to create the interface endpoints and route tables so our infra team can validate?
[05:45] Priya Nair: Absolutely - that's part of what I'll share. We have example CloudFormation and Terraform snippets for PrivateLink, peering, Transit Gateway attachments, security group rules, and route table entries.
[05:58] Samantha Lee: Pricing question: how does Private pricing differ from Dedicated or hosted? We're trying to estimate TCO.
[06:05] Alex Chen: Private has a base platform/operational fee plus resource usage and bandwidth charges. Dedicated is more of a capacity reservation with a committed spend that tends to be more predictable for high-volume use. Hosted is usage-based. I'll send a TCO sheet comparing them with sample workloads.
[06:21] Marta Gomez: Any compliance pack? SOC2, ISO artifacts? We need to hand those to procurement.
[06:27] Alex Chen: We have SOC2 and ISO documents and an enterprise security pack. For Private we'll also provide architecture and runtime hardening docs. I'll attach those in the follow-up.
[06:36] Raj Patel: A nitty-gritty: we have an internal service that relies on multicast-style internal DNS resolution across VPCs; not sure that maps cleanly to peering or PrivateLink.
[06:46] Priya Nair: Yeah, that can be tricky. Peering keeps L3 connectivity so multicast-like behavior is more feasible, but PrivateLink is L3+ overlay using ENIs so some patterns won't work. We can map your dependency and propose a pattern; sometimes a transit VPC or proxy solves those issues.
[07:04] Samantha Lee: Data residency again - if we need EU-only for a dataset, can Redwood guarantee no egress from EU cluster?
[07:12] Priya Nair: We can configure routing and access controls so EU data stays in-region. We'll also set up a separate key policy and storage buckets in region. Our security team will need to confirm operational controls.
[07:24] Marta Gomez: About logging and retention: we need 7 years for certain audit trails. Is that supported?
[07:29] Alex Chen: We can push logs to your S3 and you control lifecycle. We'll surface retention best practices for event logs and model artifacts.
[07:40] Evan Brooks: Are there limits on concurrent connections for the private endpoints? We have bursty traffic.
[07:46] Priya Nair: There are connection limits per ENI for PrivateLink; we recommend load distributing across multiple endpoints/subnets. For peered setups the limits are driven by our ingress autoscaling - we autoscale worker pools and can accommodate bursts if the topology allows. We'll share recommended subnet and endpoint counts.
[08:06] Raj Patel: What about software updates/patching for the private control plane? We can't have downtime during office hours.
[08:13] Alex Chen: We support rolling upgrades and can schedule maintenance windows. For high-availability we recommend active/active pairs or can run canary upgrades and fallback.
[08:25] Samantha Lee: Is there a way to test network performance before cutover? A quick smoke test or benchmark?
[08:31] Priya Nair: Yes, we can run a connectivity test and a small-scale perf benchmark from your infra to a staging private deployment. We'll coordinate IP whitelists and run token-limited workloads.
[08:44] Marta Gomez: On IAM, we need service principals and short-lived tokens.
[08:49] Priya Nair: We support short-lived credentials and map service principals to roles in the control plane. SCIM + SAML for people and token exchange for services.
[08:58] Raj Patel: Any pitfalls with GCP or Azure vs AWS? Our primary infra is multi-cloud.
[09:04] Priya Nair: Patterns are similar but details differ. GCP's VPC peering has no transitive peering; Azure has Private Endpoint model comparable to PrivateLink. Region-to-region connectivity and managed GPU availability varies; some regions may lack the specific GPU instance types we recommend. If you're multi-cloud, often the pattern is to deploy regionally where the workloads live and use self-serve peering in each cloud.
[09:29] Samantha Lee: Okay. Can you summarize recommended topology for us?
[09:33] Priya Nair: Given your tight CIDR space and security constraints, our recommended first pass is PrivateLink (interface endpoints) in your VPC in us-east-1 for production traffic, plus a separate EU deployment with its own PrivateLink endpoints for EU data. If you later want lower latency or broader network access, we can evaluate a transit gateway peering model.
[09:56] Alex Chen: That sounds right. We'll send a diagram for the PrivateLink setup and one for Transit Gateway peering so you can compare.
[10:04] Samantha Lee: Great. A few quick follow-up items from our side: we'll share CIDR ranges and compliance questionnaire.
[10:10] Marta Gomez: Also want to schedule a deeper technical session with your SEs to walk packet flows and DNS setup.
[10:16] Alex Chen: We can do that - Priya, available next week?
[10:19] Priya Nair: Yes, I can do a deeper dive. I'll propose slots.
[10:23] Raj Patel: Last thing - latency SLOs. We need 99th percentile under 120ms for our chat inference path.
[10:30] Priya Nair: That's reasonable if the deployment is in-region and the model size fits a low-latency profile. We'll provide benchmark numbers for models and sequence lengths similar to yours.
[10:42] Samantha Lee: Ok thanks everyone. We'll expect the docs and sample configs.
[10:47] Alex Chen: Thanks - we'll follow up with pricing, network diagrams, infra snippets, SOC2/ISO, and schedule the deep dive.
[10:55] [Meeting ends]

Note: transcript contains occasional auto-transcribe artifacts (e.g., "kayvee cash" instead of KV cache, "private link" vs PrivateLink casing). Links referenced during call: internal security pack (link: /redwood/security-pack.pdf), terraform examples repo (link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-examples).
